c1.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — Platform & Dashboard Command
c1.desc: Access, sessions, and the dashboard mastered to the formula level: role-based views, every KPI card's calculation, timeframe mechanics, every chart — and what to train each client role to look at.

lessons.title: Access, credentials, and sessions — what you'll support daily
lessons.html:
Half of week-one support tickets are access. Know this cold.

Login requirements: an account (created by the admin — the user receives a welcome email or credentials from their manager), the tenant URL, a modern browser (Chrome 90+, Firefox 88+, Edge 90+, Safari 14+ — Internet Explorer is not supported), and internet. First login may force a temporary-password change, show a welcome tour, and prompt profile completion.

The failure modes and their fixes: "Invalid email or password" — typos, Caps Lock, or an old password; after repeated failures (typically 5) the account locks for 15–30 minutes, or an administrator unlocks it immediately. "Session expired" — inactivity timeout (typically 30 minutes–2 hours; 'Remember Me' extends to 7–30 days); just log in again, and warn users that unsaved form data is lost on expiry. Page won't load — connection, wrong URL, cache clear, or another browser, in that order.

Forgot Password, precisely: the reset link goes only to the exact email on the account; the system deliberately never confirms whether an email exists (anti-enumeration); the link expires (typically 24h, sometimes 1h) and is single-use — closing the page mid-reset means requesting a fresh link. Email not arriving: spam folder → wait 1–5 min → verify the address → IT mail logs → admin manual reset, in that order. Password policies commonly enforce 8+ characters, case + number variety, sometimes specials, no reuse of the last ~5, no dictionary words.

Sessions and multi-device: each device holds its own independent session; changes sync across them in real time; logging out on one does not log out others; concurrent-session caps (where configured) terminate the oldest. Some tenants expose Active Sessions under account/security settings — the "terminate that device and change your password" flow is your stolen-phone playbook. Password change keeps the current session alive; other sessions may die immediately or at natural expiry per configuration.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client's staffer calls: "locked out, reset email never came." Give the five-step sequence you run before touching the admin panel — spam, wait, exact-address check, IT mail logs, then admin manual reset. And the question you ask FIRST: "which email did you type?" — the anti-enumeration design means a wrong address fails silently.

lessons.title: The dashboard — layout, hierarchy, and role-based views
lessons.html:
The dashboard answers the critical questions within seconds of login: revenue, pipeline volume, channel performance, agent targets — one scrollable page, no report-hopping. Its structure, top to bottom: the global timeframe filter (controls every metric and chart on the page), the KPI cards row (4–6 headline numbers with comparison indicators), the Revenue Trend chart, the Channel Mix donut, the Top Products table, the Agent Leaderboard, and a Recent Activity feed (order status changes, new customers, campaign events — some elements live-update via WebSocket; otherwise refresh the page for fresh numbers).

The dashboard is role-shaped, and you must know all four shapes because you will train all four:

  1. Closers see only themselves: My Orders Today, My Delivered Orders, My Conversion Rate, My Revenue, personal trend and status distribution. No team data, no other agents — focus by design.
  2. Team Managers see aggregates (Total Team Revenue/Orders, Team Conversion, AOV) plus the Agent Leaderboard prominently, Channel Mix, Top Products — the coaching and rebalancing view.
  3. Marketing sees the funnel: Total Submissions, Campaign Conversion Rate, Cost Per Lead, ROAS, submission trends, channel attribution, and a Campaigns Summary table.
  4. Directors/Admins see everything, with drill-down from any element.

The dashboard is a navigation hub, not a poster: clicking a KPI card opens the matching list pre-filtered to the same date range; clicking a trend bar filters orders to that day; clicking a leaderboard name opens that agent's profile. Teach clients the habit: red indicator → click it → investigate, instead of red indicator → meeting.

The working rhythm to install at every client: start each session on 'Today', switch to 'This Week'/'This Month' for trend; managers check first thing morning and last thing evening; leaderboard on screen during team meetings.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client's marketing lead complains "the dashboard is useless — it's all sales numbers." Diagnosis? Their user carries the wrong role; the dashboard is role-shaped, so the fix is role assignment, not customization. Verify what role their account holds before anything else.

lessons.title: KPI cards — every formula, and reading them as a set
lessons.html:
Each card: one bold number, a label, a comparison indicator vs. the equivalent previous period, sometimes a sparkline. The four core cards, at formula level:

CardFormula / basisThe trap to teach
Total RevenueSum of orders reaching Delivered in the period; returns are subtractedIt is realized revenue only — in-progress and cancelled orders are excluded
Total OrdersCount of orders created in the period, ANY statusVolume, not success — read with Conversion and AOV, never alone
Conversion Rate(Delivered ÷ Total Orders) × 10060% = 6 of 10 delivered; the rest cancelled, failed, returned, or still moving
Average Order ValueTotal Revenue ÷ Delivered OrdersFalling AOV with rising volume can mean discounting is buying the growth

The comparison indicator always matches like with like: 'This Week' compares to last week, 'This Month' to last month — and mid-period it compares equivalent elapsed spans (Wednesday of this week vs. Monday–Wednesday of last week). Green +12% / red −5%. Early in a day or month, extreme percentages are normal — small denominators, teach calm.

Worked read: Revenue AED 125,000 (+8%), Orders 342 (+15%), Conversion (−4pts), AOV (−3%). The set says: volume is up strongly but conversion and value both slipped — marketing is buying more but weaker leads, or ops can't keep pace. Revenue's +8% alone would have said "all good"; the set says "investigate lead quality." That is the reading discipline: never one card in isolation.

Role-scoped cards: managers may additionally see Pending (New Lead/Qualified/Confirmed awaiting processing), In Progress (Assigned/Processing/Delivery In Progress), Completed — pipeline-health at a glance; a swelling Pending card is a bottleneck announcement. Closers see the My-* variants of all four cores, scoped to their own orders.

Interpretation heuristics to hand clients verbatim: improving conversion from 55%→60% on 1,000 monthly orders at AED 300 AOV = 50 extra deliveries = AED 15,000/month — small percentage points are real money. All-green = healthy; mixed = targeted attention; all-red = immediate investigation.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Client MD: "revenue says 125k but my bank got 90k this month — your system is wrong." Name the two honest explanations before defending anything: Delivered-basis vs cash timing (COD collections and settlements lag), and returns subtracted after delivery. The card measures delivered order value, not bank receipts.

lessons.title: Timeframes — the filter that rules the page
lessons.html:
The date selector sits top-right and drives everything simultaneously — cards, charts, leaderboard, feed. The presets and their exact behavior:

PresetWindowCompares againstTrend granularity
TodayMidnight → nowYesterday's equivalentHourly bars
YesterdayPrevious calendar dayDay beforeHourly
This Week (default at login)Monday → todaySame days last weekDaily bars
Last WeekFull Mon–SunWeek beforeDaily
This Month1st → todaySame dates last monthDaily
Last MonthFull previous monthMonth beforeDaily
This QuarterQuarter start → todaySame span prior quarterWeekly bars
This YearJan 1 → todaySame span last yearMonthly bars
CustomAny start/end via picker—Varies

Two support-call facts: very large custom ranges load slowly (aggregation volume — steer long-range analysis to the Reports section instead), and 'Today' at 8am shows tiny numbers with wild comparison percentages — normal, not broken.

Meeting rhythms to install: weekly team meetings — 'This Week' for progress, then 'Last Week' for the complete picture; monthly reviews — 'This Month' progress + 'Last Month' completed. The mid-period equivalent-span comparison is what makes 'This Week on a Wednesday' honest — teach that explicitly, because managers who don't know it distrust the numbers.

CONSULTANT DRILL: "The dashboard was fine yesterday, today everything collapsed 80%!" — First check before any escalation? The timeframe selector: they're on 'Today' at 9am comparing against a full yesterday, or someone switched the preset. The filter rules the page; verify it before believing the page.

lessons.title: The charts — reading, interaction, cross-reads
lessons.html:
Revenue Trend — the page's largest element: revenue over time, granularity per the timeframe (hourly→daily→weekly→monthly). Hover any bar for exact revenue + delivered count ("AED 18,500 — 42 orders"); click a bar to open orders filtered to that period. Read for pattern: steady bars = stability; left-to-right climb = growth; dips = holidays/weekends/ops issues; spikes = campaigns. Some configurations overlay the previous period as a lighter line — comparison without switching.

Channel Mix — donut of order distribution by acquisition channel (Phone, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, Website, Referral, Walk-in, Other), total in the center, hover for exact counts ("WhatsApp: 145 orders (38%)"). The strategic read is the shift over time: Phone 60%→30% while WhatsApp 15%→45% across six months means the customer base migrated — processes and staffing should follow. Heavy ad spend on a channel showing a sliver = re-evaluate the spend.

Top Products — ranked by revenue (or units): name, units, revenue, share. New entrant in the top 5 = demand signal; a stalwart dropping off = stock, season, or competitor. Hover for average selling price and unique buyers; click for that product's orders.

Agent Leaderboard (managers+) — rank, name, total orders, delivered, conversion, revenue; medals for top three and rank-trend arrows in some configurations. Uses: recognition, coaching targets, and workload signals (one agent carrying double the orders = redistribute). Click a name → their profile/orders.

Campaign Performance (marketing view) — per campaign: submissions, orders, conversion, revenue, CPA where cost is entered. High-submission/low-conversion = targeting or offer problem; low-volume/high-conversion/high-revenue = efficient reach — scale it.

Cross-reads to teach explicitly: Trend + Channel Mix = how much AND from where; Top Products + Leaderboard = are the best agents selling different things (share the playbook); Campaign Summary + Channel Mix = does spend align with what actually drives orders. Empty chart = no records in the timeframe — widen the range before filing a bug.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Design the five-minute Monday ritual you'd write into a client's SOP using only this page: This Week → cards as a set → trend vs overlay → channel shift vs last month → leaderboard extremes top and bottom → one drill-down on the worst indicator. Rituals, not features, are what make CRM adoption stick.

c2.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — Orders, Customers & Fulfilment
c2.desc: The order engine mastered: list operations, creation with duplicate detection, all thirteen statuses and their transitions, the details drawer, item rules by status, assignment logic, and the customer directory with its quick actions.

lessons.title: The orders list — search, filters, and who sees what
lessons.html:
Orders is the operational heart. Visibility is role-scoped from the first pixel: closers see only their assigned orders; managers and directors see everything. Teach that before any "orders are missing" ticket.

Columns, left to right: Order ID · Customer Name · Phone Number · Status (color-coded badge) · Channel (lead source) · Amount · Agent · Created Date. Column widths drag-resize.

Search matches multiple fields at once, live as you type, case-insensitive, no Enter needed: customer name (partial fine), phone (partial — '0551' matches any number containing it), order ID (jumps straight there), and city. It beats paging through results every time — teach search-first.

The filters: Status — multi-select across all thirteen statuses, with an active-count badge on the button; the classic triage combination is New Lead + Not Reachable + Call Back = the unresolved pipeline in one view. Channel — Phone, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, Website, Referral, Walk-in, Other (marketing's evaluation lens). Date — presets or custom, on created date. Agent (managers only) — one agent's pipeline, for reviews and load checks. Clear Filters/Reset wipes everything including search.

Sorting: click any header — once ascending, again descending, arrow shows direction; default is Created Date descending. Pagination: 25 or 50 rows per page, total-matching count displayed beside the controls.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Build the "morning triage view" you'd train every client team lead to open first: Status = New Lead + Not Reachable + Call Back, Date = This Week, sorted oldest-first. That one saved habit — oldest unresolved lead first — is worth more than an hour of feature demonstration.

lessons.title: Creating an order — every field, and the duplicate check
lessons.html:
New Order (top-right of Orders) opens the creation dialog. Field by field, with the traps:

  1. Customer Name — type and the system searches existing customers; selecting a match auto-fills phone, email, and address. Search-before-create is the iron rule: duplicate customer records fragment order history forever. Similar name in suggestions? Verify by phone number.
  2. Phone Number — required, with country code, format-validated. An error here means an unreachable customer, a failed confirmation, a wasted delivery — the single most consequential field on the form.
  3. The duplicate check — when focus leaves the phone field, the system quietly compares against prior orders inside the configured detection window. Numbers are normalized to the last 10 digits, so 08012345678 and +2348012345678 are the same customer. A match raises an amber banner — prior order's ID, date, items — informational, not blocking: legitimately new order → tick 'Proceed anyway' and continue; true duplicate → close and work the existing order. Note for setup: the check on manual orders only runs if Settings → Duplicate Order Detection → 'Run on Manual Orders' is enabled — a configuration item on your implementation checklist.
  4. Email — optional but its absence disables email-based journey messages to this customer.
  5. Lead Channel — the ORIGINAL source (Phone/WhatsApp/Instagram/Facebook/Website/Referral/Walk-in/Other), set once at creation and not changed after, even if later conversation moves channels. This field is what makes every attribution report true or false.
  6. Items — Add Item → pick Category first (filters the product list) → Product (default price auto-fills, overridable for discounts) → Quantity; line total computes; repeat per product; order total sums live.
  7. Delivery Address — Street + Country/State/City as searchable combo-boxes (type 'lag' → Lagos); countries without a state dataset fall back to free text; selecting a country resets State and City, selecting a State resets City. For COD, address precision is revenue protection — confirm building and apartment.
  8. Delivery Agent — optional combo (sourced from the Agents directory; missing agent = add there first); assignable later from the drawer.
  9. Notes — context visible to all agents and managers: "morning delivery", "price-sensitive — no upsell", "Arabic only".

On Submit: status New Lead; the customer record is created or updated; auto-assignment rules may fire; journeys with an Order-Created trigger enroll the customer; the order tops the list.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client complains "the duplicate warning doesn't block anything — what's the point?" Give the design answer: repeat purchases by the same customer are legitimate and common; blocking would break real business. The banner converts silent duplication into an informed decision, and 'Proceed anyway' leaves an audit trace of that decision.

lessons.title: The thirteen statuses — lifecycle, owners, and transitions
lessons.html:
Status drives everything: visibility, responsibility, KPI math, journey automation. The happy path: New Lead → Qualified → Confirmed → Assigned → Processing → Delivery In Progress → Delivered — and the system enforces valid transitions (New Lead cannot jump to Delivered). Every status, with its owner and required action:

StatusMeansOwner / action
New LeadJust created (manual, form, or API); unreviewed raw demandManagers/leads (or auto-assignment): qualify or disqualify
QualifiedReviewed: legitimate, contactable, products available, address serviceableQualification gate passed → contact for confirmation
ConfirmedCustomer explicitly confirmed items, prices, address — serious buyerThe contacting agent updates it; order proceeds to assignment/fulfilment
AssignedAllocated to a specific closer (manual or rules)The assigned agent owns it end-to-end
ProcessingActively fulfilling: packing, labels, logistics coordinationAgent + fulfilment team → hand to delivery
Delivery In ProgressPhysically dispatched, in transitCourier; agent monitors → Delivered / Failed / Rescheduled
DeliveredThe positive terminal: received, COD collected. Counts as revenue; triggers post-delivery journeysLogistics or delivery-integration confirms
CancelledDeliberately terminated pre-delivery (mind change, stock-out, junk lead) — record the reasonNo revenue; counts in volume → hurts conversion; high rates = lead-quality signal
FailedDelivery ATTEMPTED and unsuccessful (absent, wrong address, refused, couldn't pay)Investigate: recover via reschedule/address fix, or cancel
ReturnedAccepted then sent back (defect, wrong item, remorse) — revenue reversedProcess return, inspect, restock, refund/replace
On HoldTemporarily paused (restock wait, payment verification, customer delay)Resolve the reason; never a parking lot — flag for follow-up
Not ReachableContact attempted, no answer — NOT cancelled, awaiting retryRetry policy: typically 3–5 attempts over 2–3 days, then cancel
Call BackReached; asked for a later call — still interested; note the preferred timeCall at the agreed time → Confirmed or Cancelled
RescheduledDelivery date must change (customer request, logistics, failed attempt)Coordinate new date → back to Delivery In Progress on dispatch

Branch rules: most pre-delivery stages can branch to Cancelled / On Hold / Not Reachable / Call Back; after Delivery In Progress the exits are Delivered / Failed / Rescheduled; after Delivered, only Returned. The KPI mapping to keep straight: Delivered = revenue; Returned = revenue reversed; Cancelled/Failed = no revenue but in the volume denominator, dragging conversion. That mapping is why status discipline IS reporting accuracy.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Distinguish Cancelled vs Failed vs Not Reachable in one line each — terminated by decision pre-delivery / delivery attempted and unsuccessful / contact attempted and pending retry. Clients blur these three constantly, and every blur corrupts a different report.

lessons.title: The details drawer — anatomy, timeline, and actions
lessons.html:
Click any order row → the drawer slides from the right, list still interactive behind it (click another row to switch orders; close via X, outside-click, or Escape).

Top to bottom: Header — Order ID, status badge (green = positive outcomes, yellow/orange = in motion, red = negative), creation date, channel icon. Customer Information — name (click → customer profile), phone (click → call/copy), email, city. Order Items — line table (product, category, unit price, qty, line total) with the Order Total beneath. Delivery Address — formatted block; some configurations add a map preview or Google-Maps link. Agent Assignment — current owner, or 'Unassigned' with an Assign control (managers reassign here). Notes — chronological, each with author and date. Status Timeline — every status change, newest at top: the status, the timestamp, and who made the change — the complete audit trail.

Action buttons are context-sensitive: Update Status (only valid next statuses offered), Assign/Reassign, Add Note, Edit Items, Print/Export — and a grayed button means that transition is invalid from the current status, not broken. Teach that sentence; it eliminates a whole ticket category.

The timeline is the troubleshooting tool. "Customer says the order took two weeks" — the timeline shows Confirmed on the 3rd, Assigned on the 3rd, Processing on the 4th, Delivery In Progress on the 11th: the bottleneck was fulfilment, not sales, with names and timestamps attached. Every escalation conversation starts there.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A manager insists an agent "never worked" an order. Where's the objective answer, and what does it show? The Status Timeline — every transition, its time, and the person who made it. The drawer ends who-did-what arguments; train managers to open it before opening disputes.

lessons.title: Editing items — recalculation, locks, and COD care
lessons.html:
In the drawer's Items section: Add Item (Category first → Product → price auto-fills → override if discounting → Quantity; line total live), edit quantity in place (totals recalc instantly), delete via the row's trash icon (brief confirm, totals recalc). Price overrides are logged for audit; significant discounts follow manager-approval policy — many organizations cap discount percentages.

The status lock: items edit freely in New Lead, Qualified, Confirmed. From Processing / Delivery In Progress, changes may require manager approval or be locked entirely — a physical shipment may already exist. The escape hatch for a genuine late change: move the order On Hold first, adjust, then resume. Removing items from confirmed orders = inform the customer first, always.

The COD trap, explicitly: any change to the total after confirmation means the courier will collect a different amount than the customer heard. Re-contact and re-confirm before dispatch, or the delivery fails at the door and the whole order circles through Failed. Item edits and customer communication are one motion on COD.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Agent: "the Edit Items button is grayed out — system bug." The two-step diagnosis: check the status (Processing+ locks are by design), and if a change is truly needed, the On-Hold-first route. The answer to most "bug" reports in this module is a status.

lessons.title: Assignment — manual, rules, and permissions
lessons.html:
Manual assignment: drawer → Agent section → dropdown of active closers, each showing current load ("Ahmed — 15 active orders") for balanced decisions. Selecting takes effect immediately: the Agent field updates, status may auto-advance to Assigned (from Confirmed/Qualified), the agent gets a notification, the order joins their personal list, and the timeline records who assigned, when. Reassignment is the same motion — old agent removed, new agent notified, timeline updated; but frequent reassignment confuses customers mid-conversation, so the new agent reads notes + timeline before making contact.

Auto-assignment rules (configured in Settings → Assignment Rules — an implementation-checklist item): Round Robin (even sequence), Capacity-Based (fewest active orders), Channel-Based (channel specialists), Geographic (city/region routing). Manual reassignment after auto-assignment always takes precedence — rules propose, humans dispose.

Permissions: closers cannot assign or reassign — they work what they're given; managers/team leads assign within their team; directors/admins across all teams. A disabled assign button = insufficient role, by design.

Load-balancing craft to install: check the load counts in the dropdown before every manual assignment; an agent at 30 active orders gives none of them the attention an agent at 10 gives each. Capacity discipline here connects forward to the Closer record's Max Assignment cap (Module C5) — the two mechanisms bound the same problem from both ends.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Design the assignment scheme for a client with two brands, closers specialized per brand, and one supervisor who should absorb overflow: Channel/Category-appropriate auto-rules for the specialists + the supervisor flagged Always Available with a higher cap (C5's machinery) + manual override retained for managers. Name the principle: rules propose, humans dispose.

lessons.title: Customers — directory, quick actions, and tag discipline
lessons.html:
The directory (Customers in the sidebar; role-scoped like orders): Name · Phone · Email · City · Source Channel · Total Orders · Total Spent (cumulative delivered revenue) · Last Order Date · Created Date. Universal search across name/phone/email/city (partial, live, case-insensitive — last-4-digits phone lookups work). Filters: City, Source Channel, Date Range, Tags. The three sorts that answer real questions: Total Spent desc = your VIPs; Last Order Date desc = recently active; Last Order Date asc = dormant customers ripe for re-engagement campaigns.

Quick actions on a profile — the one-click bar that prevents both wasted clicks and data errors:

  1. New Order — creation dialog pre-filled with name/phone/email/address. Always this route for existing customers — it structurally prevents duplicate customer records.
  2. WhatsApp — opens WhatsApp Web (desktop) or the app (mobile) with the number pre-filled; requires a valid number with country code.
  3. Phone — click-to-call via VoIP where integrated; otherwise copies the number / opens the native dialer.
  4. Add Note — timestamped, attributed; the habit to train: after EVERY interaction, four lines — what they wanted, what was discussed, what was promised, next action.
  5. Tags — chips added by typing + Enter, removed by X, saved instantly.
  6. Email / SMS — individual sends (templates or custom), logged to the timeline; bulk goes through Marketing → Broadcasts, never here.
  7. View All Orders — the Orders list pre-filtered to this customer.

Tag discipline is a consulting deliverable, not a feature: if half the team tags 'VIP' and half 'High Value', every tag filter lies. Facilitate an agreed vocabulary at implementation and write it down — the manual's own starter set: VIP, Wholesale, Repeat Buyer, Corporate, Influencer, Complaint, Do Not Call, Arabic Only, English Only.

c3.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — The Campaign Engine: Forms, Submissions & Carts
c3.desc: The lead-to-order machine at builder level: the three-step form wizard, category-first routing, packages and upsells, publishing and embedding, submission statuses and conversion, and the abandoned-cart lifecycle with its recovery craft.

lessons.title: Lead forms — what they are, end to end
lessons.html:
A lead form is a hosted page where a customer picks a product, enters contact and delivery details, and places an order without speaking to an agent first. It replaces the manual funnel (ads → phone/WhatsApp → agent transcribes basics) with structured capture: when the customer submits, the system already holds contact, product, quantity, and campaign source — agents confirm and close instead of collecting.

The end-to-end flow, five steps: (1) Build in the three-step wizard — Step 1 Basics (title, redirect, success message, button text, quantity display, preset country), Step 2 Builder (product category, linked products, offer packages, checkout fields, appearance), Step 3 Upsell (the optional one-more-offer screen). (2) Publish — generates a hosted link and an embed snippet. (3) The customer orders. (4) A submission appears instantly under Campaigns → Submissions, tagged with its form and any traffic-source parameters from the link. (5) Convert — an agent reviews, confirms, and one-clicks it into a CRM order that runs the normal fulfilment lifecycle.

Where forms get shared: Facebook/Instagram ads (destination URL), Google Ads (landing page), WhatsApp chats and broadcasts, SMS, email buttons, and any website page via the embed snippet.

Attribution, built in: every form is tied to the digital marketer who built it — submissions and resulting orders attribute automatically for reporting; and links carrying campaign tracking tags record the traffic source on the submission. This is the clean line from ad spend to orders that the ROAS report (C4) depends on.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client asks why they shouldn't just keep taking orders on WhatsApp. Give the three-part answer from the flow: structured capture (no transcription errors at scale), no missed leads in busy periods, and automatic attribution from ad to order — the thing manual channels can never provide.

lessons.title: Step 1: Basics — every field, and why each converts
lessons.html:
Campaigns → Lead Forms shows the list (each form: default item, digital marketer, Draft/Published status, lead count, last submission). New form opens the wizard; you can move between steps freely and Save draft anytime, resuming later from the Resume draft dropdown at the top of the builder.

  1. Form title — internal only; teach a naming convention ('Lagos Skincare Bundle - Instagram', 'March Restock Promo') so forms stay findable at fifty.
  2. Digital marketer — auto-set to the signed-in ad buyer; every submission attributes to them. Regular users cannot change it; administrators reassign by typing 4+ characters of the new owner's email.
  3. Redirect URL — optional post-submit destination (thank-you page, a WhatsApp chat link); blank = show the success message instead.
  4. Success message — set the expectation explicitly ('Our team will call within 2 hours to confirm') so customers don't resubmit.
  5. Submit button text — specific beats generic: 'Place my order' / 'Get this deal' outconverts 'Submit'.
  6. Quantity display — Number input, Dropdown, or Radio buttons; pick whichever is clearest for the offer.
  7. Preset country — 'Auto-detect from visitor IP' by default; fixing a country hides the country field entirely and records state/city under it. Fix it for single-market campaigns (e.g., Nigeria-only) — one less field is measurably fewer abandonments.
  8. Description — a short line shown above the form, or an internal note.
CONSULTANT DRILL: Rewrite this Step-1 setup for a Nigeria-only Instagram campaign: title 'form1', button 'Submit', success message 'Thanks', country auto-detect. — Title with market+offer+channel; button 'Order now' or offer-specific; success message with the callback promise and timeframe; preset country Nigeria to delete a field. Four edits, each one a conversion lever the manual names.

lessons.title: Step 2: Builder — routing, products, packages, fields
lessons.html:
Order dimensions first, and it's structural: choose one Product Category — required before publish. The Resolved Brand and Resolved Cost Center fill automatically from the category and are read-only: category-first routing is what tells the system how to file the resulting orders. (Older drafts with only a brand and no category must have a category selected to migrate.) This single dropdown is where form-building meets the client's org structure — get the category wrong and every downstream order files wrong.

Linked products: Add item → pick from the catalogue. Per product: Default quantity, one product markable as the Default option (pre-selected on open), optional image and product link. Pricing comes from the catalogue for the buyer's country — you never type prices into the form. Craft rule from the manual: best-selling or highest-margin product first, marked default.

Offer packages — quantity offers, not bundles: each package = a Package label + a Buy quantity + optional Free quantity (buy-X-get-Y-free) + either a Fixed amount or a Discount amount; one can be the default option. Built exactly for 'Buy 2, get 1 free' and 'Buy 3, save ₦2,000' — the average-order-value levers.

Core field options — every form carries the built-in checkout set: Full Name, Email, Phone, Address Line 1, Address Line 2, Country, State/Province, City, Postal Code, Notes. Per field you can edit the label, toggle Required, toggle Visible. The conversion law, verbatim from the source: shorter forms convert better — only require what you truly need at submission; collect the rest on the confirmation call.

Additional questions — for anything the built-ins don't cover: label + field type (text, email, phone, dropdown, longer text area) + required toggle. The canonical use: 'How did you hear about us?'

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client's form requires all ten core fields plus three custom questions, and its abandonment runs 65%. Which manual principles are being violated, and what's the redesign? Shorter-forms law (hide Address Line 2, Postal Code, Notes; unrequire Email), preset country if single-market, move the three questions to the confirmation call. Target: the fewest fields that let an agent complete the sale by phone.

lessons.title: Appearance, preview, publish — and the upsell screen
lessons.html:
Appearance (Step 2 panel): Button background/text colours, Page and Card backgrounds, Heading colour, Input border colour, Input border radius (e.g., 10px), Font family with preview. The trust principle: a form in the same colours as the ad the customer clicked converts better — reuse the established brand palette, keep text contrast readable.

Live preview: 'Open live preview' renders the real form in a separate tab from current builder settings; it updates as you edit (Refresh preview if not). Interact like a customer — select, adjust quantity, fill fields. And the mobile law: most lead-form traffic is mobile — narrow the window to phone width and confirm comfort before publishing.

Step 3: Upsell — the optional one-more-offer screen between the main order and final confirmation. Enable it, then configure: the Upsell item from the catalogue, an Upsell heading ('One more offer for your order'), description, optional uploaded image; presentation controls — form width, text colour, Button text ('YES, ADD TO MY ORDER'), Decline text ('No, I do not want this additional offer'), optional Scarcity line ('Only a few left'). Accept = item added to the order; decline = original stands; the decision is recorded so acceptance rates are measurable. Craft rule: a complementary add-on at a fair price is accepted far more often than an unrelated item.

Publish: requires a product category + at least one main product. Publishing makes the form live and generates the hosted link (ads, WhatsApp, SMS, email) and the embed snippet (paste into any page's HTML; builders that reject raw HTML take it via their Custom-HTML/Embed block — submissions flow identically either way). Final live-preview check of products, prices, fields, and button before every publish.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Design the upsell for a form selling a skincare set: complementary (the matching night cream, not an unrelated gadget), fair price, heading naming the benefit, scarcity line only if true. Then name the metric that judges it: the recorded accept rate — upsells are an experiment with a built-in scoreboard.

lessons.title: Submissions — the cards, five statuses, and the one-click convert
lessons.html:
Campaigns → Submissions: four summary cards — Total Submissions, Conversions, Conversion Rate, Top Form — over the table, newest first. The timespan control (Daily / Weekly / Monthly / Custom From-To) drives cards and table together. Filters: Status and Lead Form (essential when several campaigns run at once). Columns: customer + auto-generated reference, contact details, form, status badge, submitted time, linked Order once converted, and the Action button. Refresh pulls the latest; Previous/Next page through.

The five statuses:

  1. New — just arrived, unactioned; set automatically on submission. Highest priority: leads contacted within the first few minutes convert far better — and New is the only status offering the one-click Convert.
  2. Contacted — reached out, awaiting a final answer; the in-progress marker.
  3. Converted — turned into a CRM order (set automatically by the Convert action); the Order column links it; all further work happens on the order.
  4. Lost — no order resulted. Also set automatically when an order could not be created from a submission — so Lost entries deserve review for manual handling.
  5. Duplicate — flagged as a repeat, typically by phone match (optionally items) against recent orders in a short window; review against the original and work the accurate record.

Convert mechanics: glance-check the lead, click Convert — the system creates the order, copies customer and product details, links order↔submission, flips status to Converted, shows the new order number. One-time per submission: a customer's later additional purchase = a new order from Orders, never a re-convert. Post-conversion changes (items, address, cancellation) happen on the order, not the submission — the submission is a historical record; the order is the live one.

Reading the numbers into action (the manual's own decision table): low volume + high conversion = quality leads, buy more of them; high volume + low conversion = check lead quality, follow-up speed, price fit; New leads accumulating = the team isn't working leads fast enough; rising Lost/Duplicate = lead quality or forms inviting double-submission.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Write the shift-start SOP line this lesson dictates: "Set Status filter = New; work oldest first; speed of first contact is the single biggest driver of conversion." Then the follow-up habit: anything reached without an answer flips to Contacted so the New view stays a true to-do list.

lessons.title: Abandoned carts — the lifecycle and what the list shows
lessons.html:
An abandoned cart = a visitor opened a form, interacted — chose a product, started typing details — and left without submitting. Page views alone create nothing; interaction starts the tracking, and data captures progressively as they type: product selections, quantity changes, cart value, contact fields, timestamps.

The three-state lifecycle: Active — the session is open or recent, still building. Abandoned — the session went quiet: marked in the background after roughly 30 minutes idle, by a scheduled periodic check — so a just-closed tab takes a short while to appear; teach that before the "carts are delayed" ticket. Submitted — the cart became an order (the visitor returned, or your team recovered it) and leaves the follow-up queue.

Which carts you see: only those with both a name AND a phone number — actionable ones; nameless/phoneless sessions are cleared automatically rather than cluttering the list. Digital marketers see carts from their own forms only.

Resumes: a visitor returning to the form reopens their cart and increments a Resumes counter. Several resumes = a strong buying signal — the customer keeps coming back; call them promptly.

The table (Campaigns → Abandoned Carts): Contact (name, phone, email where given), Items selected, Campaign form, Abandoned relative time ('2h ago'), Resumes, Actions (Convert / Delete). Filters: From/To dates (the daily last-24h routine) and Campaign Form; search by name, phone, or email — the "customer just called about something they half-ordered" lookup.

Why recovery is the highest-ROI activity on the platform: the ad money is already spent, the interest is already demonstrated on specific products, and recovery costs one call or message — no new spend. Speed rules: fresher interest recovers far better.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client checks the cart list at 9am and complains a cart their customer mentioned at 8:45 isn't there. Two explanations from the lifecycle: the ~30-minute idle threshold + periodic background check hasn't classified it yet (still Active), or the visitor never entered both name and phone so it will never appear. Neither is a bug.

lessons.title: Cart recovery — prioritisation, outreach, conversion
lessons.html:
Prioritise by freshness and intent: recent carts and multi-resume carts first — the manual's framework in full: P1 high value + phone + within 2 hours (drop everything); P2 any value + phone + within 24h; P3 high value + phone + 1–7 days (expect lower yield); P4 email-only → automated sequence territory; no contact info → analytics value only. The speed law, verbatim in spirit: a follow-up within 15 minutes recovers 3–5× more than one after 24 hours — and within the first hour beats a day later decisively.

Prepare before contacting: open the cart — exactly which products, the cart value, how far they got, which form and campaign brought them. The conversation should feel like help, not targeting.

Channel craft: WhatsApp for most Nigerian customers — 90%+ open rates, low friction; short message naming the specific product and offering to finish the order. Phone for high-value carts — brief, helpful, named product, offer to complete over the phone. SMS as fallback with a direct form link. And the respect rule: a customer who declines is thanked and never contacted about that cart again — aggressive follow-up damages the brand and can violate communication regulations.

Converting: click Convert on the cart — the Create Order dialog opens pre-filled with name, phone, email, and the cart's items, already tagged as an abandoned-cart recovery; confirm details, create; the cart moves to Submitted and links to the order. Delete clears carts you'll never work (clear mistakes, exhausted contacts) — and a converted cart cannot be deleted, so recovered records stay intact.

The operating rhythm to install: a fixed daily block (e.g., the first 30–45 minutes of a shift) filtering the last 24 hours; consistent follow-up produces consistent recovered revenue — sporadic effort produces sporadic results. Do the arithmetic with the client: 100 abandoned carts/week × ₦20,000 average × 15% recovery = ₦300,000/week that was already paid for.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Draft the two-line WhatsApp recovery message for a cart holding 2× Vitamin C serum, abandoned 40 minutes ago: name the person, name the product, offer help finishing, add one honest sweetener if policy allows ("free delivery today"). Then name what you checked before sending: the Resumes count and the session detail — a three-resume cart gets a call, not a text.

lessons.title: The report directory — categories, roles, and the universal date filter
lessons.html:
Reports (left sidebar) opens the directory — every report as a card, grouped:

CategoryReports
SalesCloser Summary · Team Performance · Orders Status
MarketingROAS · Channel Attribution · Campaign Form Funnel · Digital Marketer Leads
ProductProduct Sales Analysis
CustomerRevenue Cohort Trends
OperationsBranch Performance · Fulfillment Health
After-SalesAfter-Sales Summary · Upsell/Cross-Sell

Role-based visibility — the answer to every "report is missing" ticket: closers typically see their own Closer Summary (and possibly Team Performance read-only); team leads see team-level with drill-down into their own team; sales managers see all sales + operations reports; marketing managers see the marketing set; operations managers see Fulfillment Health and Branch Performance; admins/executives see everything. Missing report = check the role before anything else.

The universal date filter tops every report: presets Today / Yesterday / This Week / Last Week / This Month / Last Month / This Quarter / Last Quarter / This Year / Last Year, plus custom start–end for precise windows (a promo period, exactly). Comparison mode, where offered, is a 'Compare' toggle that shows the period side-by-side against the previous one with percentage-change indicators — the difference between "revenue was 4M" and "revenue was 4M, down 12%".

CONSULTANT DRILL: Map each client role to its two must-read reports and a cadence, as an implementation deliverable: closers — own Closer Summary weekly; team leads — Closer Summary daily + Team Performance weekly; marketing — ROAS weekly + Channel Attribution monthly; MD — Team Performance + Cohorts monthly. A report library without a reading schedule is furniture.

lessons.title: Closer Summary — every column, the red flags, the coaching reads
lessons.html:
The go-to individual-performance report: daily for team leads, weekly/monthly for managers' reviews, coaching, and incentive calculations. One row per agent:

ColumnMeaning / trap
Total OrdersOrders the agent created — raw activity. Low vs peers may be underperformance OR complex high-value accounts; context first
Delivered OrdersThe true completed-sales count
Conversion Rate(Delivered ÷ Total) × 100 — the headline efficiency metric; team average shown for comparison
RevenueDelivered order value — the bottom line
AOVRevenue ÷ Delivered — notably high AOV often marks upselling skill worth spreading
Cancellation Rate(Cancelled ÷ Total) × 100 — above 20–25% is a red flag: likely creating orders without proper customer confirmation
Response TimeAverage time to respond to new assignments/inquiries

Filters: date range, Branch (compare within a location), Team.

The reading order the manual prescribes: (1) sort by Conversion Rate — who converts efficiently; (2) cross-reference Total Orders — 90% on 10 orders is less impactful than 70% on 100; (3) check Revenue for business impact; (4) hunt outliers both directions — high performers get recognized and their methods shared, low performers get coached.

The four coaching diagnoses, verbatim craft: high orders + low conversion → coach order quality (unconfirmed entries, overselling out-of-stock); low orders + high conversion → effective but under-active, push volume; low AOV → upsell/cross-sell training; high cancellation rate → audit their creation process, listen to call recordings where available.

CONSULTANT DRILL: An agent shows 120 orders, 38% conversion, 31% cancellation, team-leading raw order count. Write the one-paragraph coaching brief: the volume is manufactured — orders entered without confirmation discipline; the 31% cancellation (red-flag threshold 20–25%) says so; the intervention is the confirmation checklist before entry, not a pep talk about closing.

lessons.title: Team Performance — aggregates and the fairness metric
lessons.html:
Side-by-side comparison of teams/branches for managers, regional directors, and executives. Per row: Team/Branch · Headcount (the context column — a team of 20 naturally out-totals a team of 5) · Total Orders · Delivered · Total Revenue · Revenue per Agent = Total Revenue ÷ Headcount · Average Conversion Rate · Top Performer · Average AOV. Filters: date range, branch, metric focus.

Revenue per Agent is the fairness metric and the manual's worked example makes it vivid: 5 agents producing 100,000 (20,000 each) are outperforming 20 agents producing 300,000 (15,000 each) — the bigger absolute number is the weaker team. Compare per-agent first, always.

The reading: (1) Revenue per Agent across teams; (2) conversion outliers → investigate root cause (lead quality? training? regional stock?); (3) the Top Performer column → study what the best are doing differently.

The three structural diagnoses: one team consistently ahead → extract and share their methods (script? lead source?); large headcount + low per-agent → overstaffed or under-utilized, consider reallocation; small team + high performance → likely at capacity, the growth case for headcount.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client MD wants to reward "the best team" and points at the highest Total Revenue row. Make the fairness argument in two sentences using per-agent math, then name what you'd check next: whether the smaller high-per-agent team is capacity-constrained — that's where the next hire pays back fastest.

lessons.title: ROAS — the formula, the profitability threshold, the budget loop
lessons.html:
The most critical marketing-budget report. Per campaign: Ad Spend (entered or imported) · Revenue Generated (delivered orders attributed via lead tracking) · ROAS = Revenue ÷ Spend · Leads Generated · CPL = Spend ÷ Leads · Cost per Order = Spend ÷ Orders (more meaningful than CPL because it prices the conversion, not the click) · Lead-to-Order Conversion = (Orders ÷ Leads) × 100. Filters: date, channel (Facebook/Google/Instagram/TikTok…), campaign type.

The interpretation bands: 1.0 = break-even on revenue — after product cost, fulfilment, and overheads, losing money; 2.0 = margin-dependent; 3.0–5.0 = good for most industries, typically profitable; >5.0 = excellent, feed it budget; <1.0 = losing on revenue itself — optimise or kill.

The theorem to carry into every client conversation: ROAS measures revenue, not profit. Profitability requires ROAS > 1 ÷ gross margin. At 50% margins the threshold is 2.0 — a 2.0-ROAS campaign there merely broke even. At 30% margins the threshold is 3.33. Compute the client's own threshold in the first reporting session and write it on the report.

The budget optimisation loop, verbatim: sort by ROAS desc → identify the top 3–5 → consider raising their budgets → identify campaigns under the profitability threshold → optimise first (targeting, creative), and if ROAS doesn't improve within 2 weeks, reduce or pause → reallocate saved budget to the top performers. A standing loop, not a one-off exercise.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Client at 40% gross margin celebrates a 2.2-ROAS campaign. Threshold = 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5 — the campaign is under water on profit despite positive-sounding revenue math. Show the calculation, then the loop: two weeks of optimisation, then reallocate.

lessons.title: Product Sales & Channel Attribution — mix, pricing signals, channel truth
lessons.html:
Product Sales Analysis — revenue by product: Name · Category · Units Sold (delivered) · Revenue · % of Total Revenue (concentration: one product at 40% = dependency risk; top-3 over 50% = diversification case) · Average Selling Price (ASP notably under list = agents discounting — investigate) · Trend arrow vs previous period · Return Rate (above 10% needs attention: quality, misleading descriptions, expectation gaps). Filters: date, category, branch (regional preferences). Role note: closers see this report restricted to orders they themselves closed — their own product mix; managers see all rows.

Reads: sort by Revenue for the generators; Trend column — growing products need stock cover, decliners need a cause (season? competitor? price?); high-return products get description/image/feedback review; new products with low sales need visibility (marketing push, agent training) before judgment.

Channel Attribution — the channel truth table: per channel (Phone, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, Website, Walk-in, Referral…): Orders · Revenue · Conversion Rate (many orders + low conversion = low-quality leads from that channel) · AOV (some channels attract higher-value customers) · Share of Total · Growth Rate vs previous period. Sort by Revenue for the value ranking, then read conversion and AOV to judge quality, not just quantity — a channel can dominate volume while a smaller one quietly delivers better customers.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Product X: 22% of revenue, ASP 18% under list, 12% return rate. Three separate findings, three separate owners: concentration (strategy), discounting drift (sales management — audit the overrides), returns over the 10% line (product/description quality). One row, three workstreams — that's what reading a report at consultant level means.

lessons.title: Revenue Cohorts — the matrix, healthy retention, warning signs
lessons.html:
The most powerful analytical tool in the library: customers grouped by first-purchase month, tracked across subsequent months — the long-term health X-ray. Used by marketing (retention campaigns, LTV), executives (customer-base health), product (do improvements move repeat purchase?), finance (forecasting from retention patterns).

The matrix: rows = cohorts ('January 2026 cohort' = everyone whose first-ever order was that month); columns = Month 0 (the first-purchase month), Month 1, Month 2…; cells = revenue OR retention rate (a toggle), colour-coded dark-high → light-low as a heatmap.

Two reading directions: left→right along a row = one cohort's behaviour over time (Month 0 highest, then reasonable retention); top→bottom down a column = are recent cohorts better or worse than older ones at the same age — the trend-of-trends.

Healthy benchmarks (of Month-0 revenue): Month 1 — 20–30% for subscription-like businesses, 10–20% for occasional-purchase; Month 3 — 15–25% / 5–15%; Month 6+ — stabilisation into the loyal core.

The two warning signs: revenue near zero after Month 0 = buy-once-never-return — the post-purchase experience is failing; each new cohort retaining worse than the last = something is deteriorating (product quality, experience, competition) and compounding quietly.

Actions: poor Month-1 → automated follow-ups, thank-you offers, next-purchase codes, recommendation emails; recent cohorts worse → find what changed (price rise? quality? lead-source mix?); recent cohorts better → identify the cause and double down.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client's matrix shows every cohort collapsing to ~2% by Month 1 — but they sell bulk 3-month supplies. Before declaring a retention crisis, name the interpretive step: benchmark against the purchase cycle. A 3-month replenishment product should show its retention pulse at Month 3, not Month 1. Cohort reading is business-model-relative.

c5.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — Administration: Closers & Shifts
c5.desc: The implementer's module: the Closer doctype end to end — the golden rule, all six blocks, creation, lifecycle, troubleshooting — and Shift Management from concept through setup, the coverage grid, the acceptance test, and rollout strategy.

lessons.title: The Closer record — what it is, and the golden rule
lessons.html:
A closer is the record representing a salesperson who works leads and orders — and almost everything revolves around it: auto-assignment targets closers, orders attribute to them, the follow-up pool draws from them, performance reports are built on them. Creating a closer correctly at onboarding is one of the highest-leverage tasks a consultant performs on a tenant.

Mechanics: doctype Closer, list at /app/closer, records auto-named CRM-CS-######, access requiring System Manager / CRM Manager. A closer record does not stand alone — it layers on a User account, adding the sales attributes (brand, categories, reporting line, capacity, availability) to a person who already has a login.

THE GOLDEN RULE: a User must exist before you can create their Closer. The first and required field on the form ("Closer") is a link that picks an existing user by email — no user account, no dropdown entry, no proceeding. The workflow is always: confirm/create the User first (Users & Permissions → User; New User with names, email, and the sales-closer role profile per standard onboarding), note the exact email, then open the Closer form.

And its corollary: one person = one user = one closer. The two steps are separate by design — the user gives identity and login; the closer gives a place in the sales structure. A duplicate closer for the same person is not allowed; if one exists, disable/merge to the correct record.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Onboarding day, a new hire's name won't appear in the Closer field dropdown. State the diagnosis without opening a ticket: their User account doesn't exist yet — the dropdown lists existing users only. Create the user, reopen the Closer form. This is the single most common closer-setup confusion, and the golden rule answers it every time.

lessons.title: Anatomy — the six blocks of a Closer
lessons.html:
The form is one scrolling page, best understood as six blocks:

BlockFields & function
A · IdentityCloser (required Link → User, by email — the golden-rule field) · Full Name (display name on leads, orders, reports) · Phone Number · Enabled (active and eligible for assignments; untick to deactivate without deleting)
B · Behaviour flagsFollow-Up Team Member — when checked, this closer can claim and convert orders from the follow-up pool. Always Available (ignore shifts) — when Shift Management is on, receives auto-assigned leads at all times regardless of schedule; for supervisors / overflow closers, and the migration default
C · PlacementCountry (Link) · Branch (Link) · Brand (multi-select — a closer can serve several brands). Placement determines which leads and orders can flow to this closer
D · ReportingReports To (Link → Closer, the direct manager) — setting it auto-fills Manager Full Name and the read-only Reporting Chain: Brand Manager, Team Manager, Cluster Manager, derived by walking up the hierarchy. Never typed by hand
E · CategoriesChild table: one row per product category the closer may work, each row tied to a brand — narrowing their remit within their brand(s). Add Row singly or Upload for bulk
F · CapacityMax Assignment — the cap on concurrent live assignments; the workload-balancing lever. Current Assignment — read-only live counter maintained by the system (0 for a new closer); never editable

Two blocks deserve emphasis. Reporting (D): the chain re-derives whenever Reports To changes anywhere up the tree — so a wrong-looking chain is fixed by correcting the manager link (on this record or above), never by editing chain fields. Capacity (F): Max Assignment is the structural end of the load-balancing you practise manually from the assignment dropdown (C2) — the cap holds even when nobody is watching the dropdown.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client asks you to "just fix" a closer whose Reporting Chain shows the wrong Team Manager. Name the only correct move and why: re-point Reports To (here or up the chain) and let the chain re-derive — the chain fields are computed, and hand-edits are impossible by design.

lessons.title: Creating a closer — the eleven steps, and the recipes
lessons.html:
The creation sequence, in order — step 1 is the golden-rule prerequisite, never skipped:

  1. Confirm the user exists (or create it first).
  2. Open a New Closer — from the CRM workspace or /app/closer → + Add Closer; the form opens "New Closer — Not Saved."
  3. Select the user in the Closer field by typing their email. Not in the dropdown = stop, create the user.
  4. Full Name and Phone Number.
  5. Tick Enabled — assignable from day one.
  6. Behaviour flags — Follow-Up Team Member if they work the pool; Always Available for supervisors/overflow.
  7. Country, Branch, Brand(s).
  8. Reports To — the manager; watch the chain auto-fill.
  9. Categories — one row per category they handle.
  10. Max Assignment — a sensible cap; leave Current Assignment alone.
  11. Save (Ctrl+S) — auto-named CRM-CS-######.

The batch trick from the manual: onboarding several closers sharing branch/brand/manager/categories — build the first fully, then duplicate it and change only the Closer (user), Full Name, and Phone per person.

The three worked recipes: Front-line closer — Enabled ON, both behaviour flags OFF (they work shifts), placement + manager + categories + the standard front-line cap. Supervisor/overflow — same, plus Always Available ON, consider a higher Max Assignment and Follow-Up Team Member ON to absorb overflow and work the pool. Offboarding — open the closer → untick Enabled → Save. Do not delete; and re-point anyone who Reports To them to a new manager.

The pre-save checklist (the manual's own): user exists and selected · name + phone · Enabled ticked · flags correct · Country/Branch/Brand set · Reports To set, chain populated · ≥1 Category row · sensible Max Assignment · saved as CRM-CS-######.

CONSULTANT DRILL: Write the two-line spec for a client's new overflow supervisor: Always Available ON (leads regardless of shifts), Follow-Up Team Member ON (works the pool), Max Assignment above the front-line cap, reporting straight to the sales head. Every choice traces to a field you can name.

lessons.title: Lifecycle & troubleshooting — disable, adjust, diagnose
lessons.html:
Everyday management from the /app/closer list (filterable by Full Name, Status, Enabled, Follow-Up membership, ID): toggle Enabled for leave/departures (stops new assignments, preserves all history); edit Categories rows as remits change; adjust Max Assignment — the engine respects the new cap immediately on save; re-point Reports To on manager moves (chain re-derives); update Country/Branch/Brand on transfers; tick Follow-Up Team Member to admit someone to the pool.

The caution that protects clients from themselves: prefer disabling over deleting. Deleting a closer can orphan the leads, orders, and reports attributed to them. Out of circulation = untick Enabled. Teach it as doctrine.

The troubleshooting table, internalized:

SymptomDiagnosis
Person missing from the Closer dropdownNo User account yet — create the user first, reopen the form
Two closer records for one personNot allowed — one user = one closer; disable/merge to the correct record
Closer gets no auto-assigned leadsThe four-point check, in order: Enabled ON? Brand/Branch/Category match the incoming leads? On shift (or Always Available)? Max Assignment not already reached?
Reporting Chain looks wrongDerived from Reports To — fix the manager link (here or up the chain), never the chain fields
Can't edit Current AssignmentBy design — a live system counter; manage load through Max Assignment

That four-point no-leads check is the single most valuable diagnostic in this module — it resolves the majority of "the system stopped giving X leads" calls without an engineer.

CONSULTANT DRILL: "Chidi hasn't received a lead all morning." Run the four checks aloud in order — Enabled, placement/category match against what's actually arriving, shift status or the Always-Available flag, capacity vs cap — and name which one the morning's evidence already rules out. Systematic beats psychic.

lessons.title: Shift Management — the concept and its rules
lessons.html:
Shift Management schedules which closers are eligible for automatic assignment of new online leads, so auto-assignment only reaches people actually on shift. Deliberately simple and self-contained — closers aren't necessarily staff with formal HR records. Off by default: until a manager enables it, assignment behaves exactly as before; turning it off again fully restores that behaviour — a true master switch.

The operating rules, each one a support-call answer:

  1. Availability follows the schedule — there is no clock-in. A closer is on shift when the current time falls inside an assigned shift for that day.
  2. Nobody on shift → the lead waits as a New Lead, unassigned; a background job re-checks about every ten minutes and assigns the moment someone comes on shift. No lead is ever lost or discarded.
  3. Always Available closers (the C5 flag) receive leads at all times regardless of schedule — supervisors and overflow.
  4. Overnight shifts: end time earlier than start (22:00–06:00) is treated as spanning midnight into the next morning.
  5. Daily limits still apply, layered on top: a closer must be BOTH on shift AND under their daily limit. And the subtlety worth teaching: the daily limit resets at midnight server time, independently of shifts — an overnight closer gets a fresh allowance mid-shift. A limit that follows the shift instead is a listed future enhancement.
  6. Online store orders are never held — routed as before; a paid order never waits on a schedule.
  7. Manual assignment always works: shifts never block a manager's hand-assignment; the closer list marks who's on shift and lists them first as a hint, but anyone remains choosable.
CONSULTANT DRILL: Three rapid-fire client questions, one-line answers each: "Do closers clock in?" — no, availability follows the schedule. "What happens to a lead at 3am with nobody scheduled?" — it waits as New Lead; the ~10-minute catch-up job assigns it when a shift starts. "Can I still give a lead to someone off-shift?" — always; shifts constrain the robot, never the manager.

lessons.title: Shifts — setup, the coverage grid, the acceptance test, rollout
lessons.html:
Setup, all on the Shifts page (left menu, visible to managers): Step 1 — switch Enable Shift Management on and leave Auto catch-up unassigned leads on (recommended — it is what picks up waiting leads). Step 2 — Shift Templates tab → New shift: name (e.g., Morning), start and end times, tick the weekdays it runs, optional colour for the grid. Step 3 — Assignments tab → Assign: pick the closer, the shift, the from-date, leaving the to-date blank for an ongoing schedule. Step 4 (optional) — mark the Always-Available people on their closer records.

Daily use — the coverage grid: a weekly grid, rows = closers, columns = days, coloured blocks = shifts; a green dot beside a name = on shift right now; arrows move between weeks, 'Today' jumps back. On an order, the closer list marks and front-sorts the on-shift people — hint, not restriction.

The nine-step acceptance test — run it at every go-live, exactly as the manual specifies: enable the feature → create a shift covering right now (started an hour ago, ends hours ahead, today ticked) → assign one closer from today → verify their green dot (and nobody else's) → create a lead: it must go to the on-shift closer, never an off-shift one → cancel that assignment and create another lead: it must wait as New Lead → re-assign a closer to an active shift: within about ten minutes the waiting lead is picked up → confirm a manager can still hand-assign an off-shift closer → turn the feature off: behaviour returns to normal, every active closer eligible again. Expected result, verbatim in spirit: on = only on-shift or always-available closers are auto-reachable; off = exactly as before.

The rollout strategy the manual recommends — and it's pure change-management wisdom: mark everyone Always Available first, then remove the flag person by person as you add their real shifts. Nothing breaks on day one; the schedule tightens gradually. Housekeeping: disable a shift rather than delete (keeps history); cancel an assignment to remove it from coverage while keeping the audit record.

The boundaries — say them before clients ask: not included yet, planned separately: per-shift lead caps (the limit is per calendar day), shift-by-shift performance reporting, clock-in/attendance, and automatic hand-off of in-progress leads at shift end — shifts affect new leads only; work already in a closer's hands stays with them.

CONSULTANT DRILL: A client wants shifts live across 14 closers next Monday. Write the plan in four lines: (1) this week — templates + assignments entered, everyone flagged Always Available; (2) Monday — feature on, run the nine-step acceptance test with one volunteer's flag removed; (3) weeks 2–3 — remove flags team by team as confidence builds; (4) set expectations on the four not-yet boundaries in writing. Rollouts fail on surprise, not on software.
